system_prompt: You are a security auditor assistant. Answer concisely, technically, and name the exact issue.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
q = "SELECT * FROM audit WHERE actor = '{}'".format(request.args['actor'])
rows = db.execute(q).fetchall()
items.reference:
LABEL: sql injection — the query is built with string formatting (.format interpolation) so the actor value can break out of the literal.
FIX: parameterized query with a bound parameter.

LABEL: sql injection — the host from the request body is concatenated into the query string.
FIX: use a parameterized/prepared statement with placeholders.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
sort_col = request.args.get('sort', 'id')
q = f"SELECT id, name FROM items ORDER BY {sort_col}"
return db.execute(q)
items.reference:
LABEL: sql injection — the sort column is interpolated into the ORDER BY clause; identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so allowlist the column name.
FIX: validate sort_col against a fixed set of allowed columns (parameterization alone cannot bind identifiers).

items.prompt:
Review this config for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
# docker-compose.yml
environment:
  - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=Sup3rS3cret!
items.reference:
LABEL: hardcoded secret — the Grafana admin password is an embedded credential in source (docker-compose file in the repo).
FIX: inject from a secret store; rotate the exposed password.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET = "8f3c1d9e2b4a4f5e8a7c6d5e4f3b2a1d"
def token_url():
    return f"https://sso.corp/token?client_secret={OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}"
items.reference:
LABEL: hardcoded secret — the OAuth client secret is committed in source; the secret in source also leaks via the token URL it is interpolated into.
FIX: load from the environment/secret manager; send secrets in the request body, never the URL; rotate.

items.prompt:
Review this YAML for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
integrations:
  pagerduty:
    routing_key: "R1O9U8T7INGKEY6543"
  datadog:
    api_key: "dd_live_4f9e2c1a8b7d"
items.reference:
LABEL: hardcoded secret — integration API keys are embedded credentials in source (committed YAML).
FIX: move to a secret manager/env injection; rotate both keys.

LABEL: command injection — the domain is concatenated into a command executed by the shell via os.system.
FIX: subprocess.run(["dig", "+short", domain], shell=False) with list arguments.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
cmd = "kubectl logs " + request.args['pod']
subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True)
items.reference:
LABEL: command injection — the pod name from the request reaches a shell=True Popen.
FIX: subprocess.run(["kubectl", "logs", pod], shell=False) and validate the pod name.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
import os
def stop_job(jid):
    os.system(f"kill -9 {jid}")
items.reference:
LABEL: command injection — the job id from user input is interpolated into a shell command (os.system).
FIX: pass the pid as a list argument with shell=False and validate it is numeric.

LABEL: arbitrary code execution — eval builds and runs a function from user input.
FIX: parse with a restricted expression parser (ast with a whitelist of nodes); never eval user text.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
code = request.json['snippet']
exec(compile(code, "<user>", "exec"))
items.reference:
LABEL: arbitrary code execution — exec runs user-supplied code directly on the server.
FIX: run untrusted code only in an isolated sandbox (separate process/container, no secrets) or replace with a declarative rule format.

LABEL: arbitrary code execution — pricing rule expressions are evaluated with eval; anyone who can edit a rule gets code execution.
FIX: use a safe expression evaluator (asteval/numexpr with restricted namespace) instead of eval.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
import hashlib
def check_login(pw, stored):
    return hashlib.new('md5', pw.encode()).hexdigest() == stored
items.reference: LABEL: weak hash — md5 is an unsalted fast hash unsuitable for passwords; replace with bcrypt or argon2 salted password hashing.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
api_key = generate_key()
stored = hashlib.sha1(api_key.encode()).hexdigest()
items.reference: LABEL: weak hash — sha1 is an unsalted fast hash; leaked digest tables are cheaply brute-forced. Fix: store only salted slow hashes (bcrypt/argon2) or HMAC-SHA256 with a server-side pepper.
LABEL: weak hash — plain sha256 is an unsalted fast hash for passwords (GPU-crackable); use a password KDF: bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt with a per-user salt.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
import aiohttp
async def fetch(url):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
        async with s.get(url, ssl=False) as r:
            return await r.text()
items.reference:
LABEL: tls verification disabled — ssl=False turns off certificate validation: mitm (man-in-the-middle) can impersonate the server.
FIX: default ssl context or a CA bundle; never ssl=False.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
import smtplib, ssl
ctx = ssl.SSLContext()
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
with smtplib.SMTP('mail.corp', 465) as s:
    s.starttls(context=ctx)
items.reference:
LABEL: tls verification disabled — CERT_NONE accepts any certificate; a mitm (man-in-the-middle) can intercept mail credentials.
FIX: keep CERT_REQUIRED and load the internal CA (load_verify_locations).

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch
es = Elasticsearch(['https://es.corp:9200'], verify_certs=False, ssl_show_warn=False)
items.reference:
LABEL: tls verification disabled — verify_certs=False skips certificate validation (mitm risk on the search cluster); ssl_show_warn=False hides it.
FIX: verify_certs=True with the CA bundle path (ca_certs).

LABEL: path traversal — os.path.join does not stop '../' segments: f=../../etc/passwd escapes /var/log/app (no containment check).
FIX: sanitize the path with basename or verify the resolved realpath stays inside the log directory.

LABEL: path traversal — the :name parameter is concatenated onto /data/public; ../ segments escape the directory.
FIX: sanitize with path.basename and assert the resolved path has /data/public as its prefix (containment).

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
from pathlib import Path
def export(user_sub, out):
    src = Path('/srv/templates') / user_sub
    out.write(src.read_text())
items.reference:
LABEL: path traversal — user_sub joins straight onto the templates root; ../ components escape the directory (no containment check).
FIX: resolve and verify src.is_relative_to(base); sanitize the path before reading.

items.prompt:
Review this JavaScript code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment.body }} />
items.reference:
LABEL: cross-site scripting (xss) — user comment rendered as raw HTML via dangerouslySetInnerHTML; payloads execute in every viewer's session.
FIX: render as text, or sanitize the HTML with a real sanitizer before inserting.

items.prompt:
Review this JavaScript code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
panel.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', serverData.html);
items.reference:
LABEL: cross-site scripting (xss) — serverData.html is inserted unparsed into the DOM; unescaped user content in it executes as script.
FIX: build DOM nodes with textContent, or escape/sanitize before insertAdjacentHTML.

items.prompt:
Review this Jinja template for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:

{{ user_bio | safe }}
items.reference:
LABEL: cross-site scripting (xss) — the |safe filter disables autoescaping, so the user bio is emitted unescaped into the page.
FIX: drop |safe and render escaped; sanitize server-side only if rich text is a requirement.

LABEL: missing access control — the endpoint returns any user's cards with no authentication and no ownership check against the session user (IDOR).
FIX: require login, scope the query to the authenticated user, and 404 cross-tenant access.

LABEL: missing access control — the admin settings endpoint has no authentication/authorization middleware; unauthorized callers read full app settings.
FIX: gate the route behind login + admin role (session check or middleware).

LABEL: missing access control — destructive delete with no login_required and no ownership/authorization check; anyone (unauthenticated) can delete any document.
FIX: require an authenticated session, verify ownership, and confirm via POST.

LABEL: insecure predictable random — API keys generated from the random module are predictable (Mersenne Twister is not crypto-secure).
FIX: secrets.token_urlsafe(24) or os.urandom — secure random only.

LABEL: insecure predictable random — OTP codes from random.randrange are predictable once the stream is observed.
FIX: secrets.randbelow(10**6) (crypto/secure random) and rate-limit verification.

LABEL: insecure predictable random — uuid1 embeds the MAC address and a timestamp, making reset tokens guessable (not a secure random source).
FIX: secrets.token_hex(32) or uuid4 (crypto-grade randomness) with single-use, short-TTL storage.

LABEL: ssrf (server-side request forgery) — the server fetches an attacker-chosen URL: internal/metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) are reachable and their content is echoed back.
FIX: allowlist target hosts, block private/link-local IPs after DNS resolution.

LABEL: ssrf — the scrape host comes from the request body: internal services and cloud metadata endpoints can be targeted from the server's network position.
FIX: allowlist the host against the registered instances; block private ranges.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
task = pickle.loads(queue.get(job_id))
run(task)
items.reference:
LABEL: unsafe deserialization — queue payloads unpickled with pickle.loads; a poisoned job message is arbitrary code execution on the worker.
FIX: serialize jobs as JSON (or signed+pickle with restricted unpickler); treat the queue as a trust boundary.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
state = marshal.loads(bytes.fromhex(request.cookies['s']))
session.update(state)
items.reference:
LABEL: unsafe deserialization — session state restored with marshal.loads from a client cookie; marshal streams can carry payloads leading to arbitrary code execution and the cookie is fully attacker-controlled.
FIX: signed JSON (HMAC) for session state; never deserialize untrusted bytes.

LABEL: open redirect — the post-logout target comes straight from the return_to parameter; //evil.com bounces users from the trusted site to a phishing page.
FIX: accept only same-origin relative paths (starts with '/' and not '//'); else default route.

LABEL: open redirect — the SAML RelayState is used as the redirect target without validation, bouncing authenticated users anywhere.
FIX: validate RelayState against the service allowlist before redirecting.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
claims = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, options={'verify_signature': False})
if claims['role'] == 'admin':
    grant_admin()
items.reference:
LABEL: jwt verification disabled — signature verification is off, so tokens (including role=admin) can be forged by anyone.
FIX: verify the signature with the correct key and pinned algorithm before reading claims.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
claims = jwt.decode(token, KEY, algorithms=['HS256', 'none'])
items.reference:
LABEL: jwt verification misconfigured — the accepted algorithm list includes 'none', so unsigned forged tokens validate.
FIX: pin algorithms to exactly the intended one (e.g., ['HS256']) and never allow none.

LABEL: permissive cors — origin:true reflects any origin while credentials are allowed: any website can make authenticated cross-origin calls and read the responses.
FIX: allowlist trusted origins; credentials only for first-party apps.

items.prompt:
Review this Flask code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
resp.headers.add('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', request.headers.get('Origin', '*'))
resp.headers.add('Access-Control-Allow-Credentials', 'true')
items.reference:
LABEL: permissive cors — the Origin header is reflected verbatim with Allow-Credentials: equivalent to '*' with credentials, enabling cross-origin data theft.
FIX: compare the origin against a server-side allowlist before echoing it.

LABEL: secrets written to logs — the password-reset token (a credential) is logged; everyone with log access can take over accounts.
FIX: log the user id and event only; never the token (or log a truncated fingerprint).

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
audit.write(f'{ts} AUTH {username}:{password} ok={ok}')
items.reference:
LABEL: secrets written to logs — the audit line includes the password: credential material flows into the log pipeline.
FIX: log username and outcome only; scrub credential fields at the logger boundary.

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
if not coupon.used_by.exists():
    coupon.used_by.add(user)
    coupon.save()
items.reference:
LABEL: race condition — check-then-act on coupon redemption without a lock or atomic constraint: parallel requests both pass the check and double-redeem.
FIX: enforce uniqueness atomically (DB unique constraint / SELECT FOR UPDATE inside a transaction).

items.prompt:
Review this Python code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
if seats_remaining > 0:
    book_seat(flight_id, user)
    seats_remaining -= 1
items.reference:
LABEL: race condition — unsynchronized check-then-act: concurrent bookings oversell the flight (counter decrement is not atomic).
FIX: atomic conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE seats_remaining > 0) in a transaction, check rowcount.

LABEL: mass assignment — fields='__all__' binds every model column from the request: is_admin/role can be set by any caller (privilege escalation).
FIX: allowlist the writable fields explicitly in the serializer schema.

items.prompt:
Review this Node code for security issues and name the exact vulnerability:
await Account.update(req.body, { where: { id: user.id } });
items.reference:
LABEL: mass assignment — the whole request body is passed to the update: plan, role, or quota fields can be modified by the client (privilege escalation).
FIX: pick an explicit allowlist of fields from req.body before updating.

items.prompt: This production Express app sets no security headers anywhere (no helmet, no manual middleware). List the HTTP security response headers it is missing and what each prevents.
items.reference: LABEL: missing security headers. strict-transport-security (hsts) prevents downgrade; content-security-policy (csp) blocks xss payloads; x-frame-options prevents clickjacking; x-content-type-options: nosniff prevents MIME confusion. All four are absent.

items.prompt: A Spring app is configured with .headers().frameOptions().disable() and no other header customization. Which header is disabled, what does that allow, and which headers are still missing?
items.reference: LABEL: missing security headers. x-frame-options is explicitly disabled → clickjacking becomes possible. strict-transport-security (hsts), content-security-policy (csp) and x-content-type-options are still missing and must be set.

items.prompt:
Review this cookie and name what is missing:
Set-Cookie: rememberme=9f8e7d; Domain=.corp.example; Max-Age=2592000
items.reference:
LABEL: cookie missing flags — rememberme is issued without Secure (sent over http), without HttpOnly (readable by any script), and without SameSite (csrf exposure).
FIX: Set-Cookie: rememberme=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax.

items.prompt: The SPA sets its session cookie from JavaScript: document.cookie = 'session=' + token + '; path=/'. What is wrong with this approach?
items.reference:
LABEL: cookie missing flags — a JavaScript-set session cookie cannot get HttpOnly (script-readable → session theft via any xss), and it is set without Secure or SameSite (csrf/downgrade exposure).
FIX: set the session cookie server-side with Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax.

items.prompt:
Review this ingress and name the exact issue:
kind: Ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /grafana
        backend: { serviceName: grafana, servicePort: 80 }
items.reference:
LABEL: admin panel over plain http — the Grafana dashboard is exposed on the http (port 80) ingress with no tls/https termination or redirect: logins cross the network in cleartext.
FIX: serve admin on https only; redirect http; restrict the route.

items.prompt:
Review this code and name the exact issue:
OPS_URL = 'http://ops.internal:8080/execute'
resp = requests.post(OPS_URL, json={'job': name}, auth=('ops', os.environ['OPS_PASS']))
items.reference:
LABEL: admin panel over plain http — an operations (admin) endpoint is called over http with basic auth: the ops credential crosses the network in cleartext.
FIX: use https with the internal CA for the ops service.

items.prompt:
Review this Apache config and name the exact issue:
<Directory /srv/app/backups>
  Options +Indexes
</Directory>
items.reference:
LABEL: directory listing enabled — Options +Indexes lets anyone enumerate the backups directory (data/source disclosure).
FIX: disable listing (Options -Indexes) and return 403 on directory URIs.

LABEL: directory listing enabled — autoindex on exposes the archive directory tree to anyone.
FIX: autoindex off; 403 on directory URIs; serve only explicit file paths.

items.prompt:
Review this Dockerfile line and name the exact issue:
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--insecure"]
# settings.py: DEBUG = True
items.reference:
LABEL: debug/stack traces exposed in production — DEBUG=True serves full stack traces and settings internals on every error page (information disclosure), and runserver is not a production server.
FIX: DEBUG=False, gunicorn/uwsgi, generic 500 pages, logs to a structured sink.

items.prompt:
Review this .env in the production deploy and name the exact issue:
APP_ENV=production
APP_DEBUG=true
LOG_LEVEL=debug
items.reference:
LABEL: debug/stack traces exposed in production — APP_DEBUG=true in production prints exceptions/stack traces to clients (information disclosure); LOG_LEVEL=debug adds verbose internal detail.
FIX: APP_DEBUG=false; raise the log level; ship traces to server-side logs only.

LABEL: no http-to-https redirect — the same app is served identically on port 80 and 443: the first request can stay in cleartext (no 301 redirect to https, no tls enforcement).
FIX: on port 80 return 301 https://$host$request_uri; add hsts on 443.

items.prompt: The load balancer terminates TLS and forwards plain http to the app; the app never checks the forwarded protocol and sets cookies with secure:false 'auto'. Name the issue.
items.reference:
LABEL: no http-to-https redirect/enforcement — after tls termination at the LB the app speaks plain http and 'auto' secure cookies downgrade on http hops.
FIX: redirect http→https at the edge (301), trust the forwarded proto, set secure cookies unconditionally.

items.prompt:
Review this header and name the exact issue:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src *; script-src * 'unsafe-inline' https:
items.reference:
LABEL: unsafe content-security-policy — csp allows every source (*, https:) plus unsafe-inline scripts: it blocks nothing and amplifies xss instead of stopping it.
FIX: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; no unsafe-inline; iterate per app.

items.prompt: A production site sends only these headers: Server: nginx, Content-Type, Date. Name what is missing.
items.reference:
LABEL: missing content-security-policy — no csp header at all (absent): inline injected scripts run unrestricted. Also missing: strict-transport-security/hsts, x-frame-options, x-content-type-options.
FIX: add the full header baseline starting with default-src 'self'.

LABEL: api over-fetch — the serializer returns every model field including password_hash, mfa_secret and internal_notes: sensitive pii/credential material leaks to any caller.
FIX: explicit allowlist schema with the minimal public fields (response model).

LABEL: api over-fetch — the public resolver returns the full user object: internal_notes and recovery data (sensitive fields) leak to unauthenticated callers.
FIX: return a minimal public schema; field-level authorization for sensitive fields.

items.prompt:
Review this manifest entry and name the exact issue:
# requirements.txt
django==3.0.1  # released Jan 2020, no patches applied since
items.reference:
LABEL: outdated dependency with known cve — django 3.0.x is end-of-life with multiple published CVEs unpatched.
FIX: upgrade to a supported patched version and pin it exactly.

items.prompt:
Review this build file and name the exact issue:
implementation 'org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core:2.14.0'
items.reference:
LABEL: outdated dependency with known cve — log4j-core 2.14.0 is in the Log4Shell range (CVE-2021-44228, JNDI remote code execution).
FIX: upgrade to 2.17.1+ and pin the version; scan transitives.

items.prompt:
Review these entries and name the exact issue:
# requirements.txt
flask-loginn==0.6.2
python-dotenv==1.0.0
items.reference:
LABEL: typosquatted package name — flask-loginn is a near-miss of flask-login; squatted packages run arbitrary code with build credentials.
FIX: install the official package from pypi (registry check), purge the lockfile entry, and rotate CI credentials.

items.prompt:
Review this package.json fragment and name the exact issue:
"dependencies": { "express": "^4.18.2", "expresss": "^1.0.3" }
items.reference:
LABEL: typosquatted package name — expresss (triple s) is not the official express package; installing it runs a stranger's code at install time.
FIX: remove the entry, verify names against the npm registry, rotate tokens the install had access to.

items.prompt:
Review this Dockerfile and name the exact issue:
FROM node:latest
COPY . /srv
RUN npm ci
items.reference:
LABEL: container image uses latest tag — builds are non-reproducible and a poisoned or broken latest pull changes production overnight.
FIX: pin a version tag or digest (node:20.x@sha256:...) — immutable, verifiable pulls.

items.prompt:
Review this k8s deployment and name the exact issue:
containers:
- name: cache
  image: redis:latest
  imagePullPolicy: Always
items.reference:
LABEL: container image uses latest tag — redis:latest with Always pull means every restart may run different upstream code; rollback is impossible.
FIX: pin the digest (immutable) and use IfNotPresent.

items.prompt:
Review this requirements.txt and name the exact issue:
flask>=2.0
requests
numpy
items.reference:
LABEL: unpinned dependency versions — only an open-ended lower bound and unpinned entries: installs are nondeterministic and a compromised future release flows in automatically (supply chain risk).
FIX: pin exact versions and commit the lockfile.

LABEL: unpinned dependency versions — '*' and open ranges with the lockfile gitignored: every build resolves differently (nondeterministic, supply chain exposure).
FIX: pin exact versions, commit package-lock.json, un-ignore it.

LABEL: no dependency audit tooling — the pipeline tests and builds but never scans dependencies: known CVEs reach production unnoticed.
FIX: add pip-audit --strict and trivy image scanning as a failing CI gate before deploy.

items.prompt: A repo has no dependabot.yml, no sbom generation, and no vulnerability scanning anywhere. What is the risk and the fix?
items.reference:
LABEL: no dependency audit tooling — with no automated scanning, sbom, or update PRs, new CVEs and compromised packages reach production silently and there is no inventory to respond with.
FIX: enable automated update PRs, add an audit gate (pip-audit/npm audit/trivy) to the pipeline, emit an sbom.

items.prompt: A core dependency had its last release 4 years ago and has 3 open CVEs with no maintainer response. What is the risk and what do you do?
items.reference:
LABEL: abandoned dependency — the package is effectively unmaintained (no release in 4 years) and its CVEs will never be fixed upstream.
FIX: plan a migration to a maintained replacement or a maintained fork; pin interim with patches backported.

items.prompt: Your direct dependencies are all clean, but a teammate says CVEs can still reach you. Through what, and how do you check?
items.reference:
LABEL: transitive dependencies — indirect packages pulled by your direct deps can carry CVEs even when your manifest is clean.
FIX: scan the full dependency tree from the lockfile (pip-audit, npm audit, dependency-tree/sbom tooling), not just declared versions.

LABEL: load-test spec defect — no stages (no ramp model), no thresholds (the test cannot fail), no checks.
FIX: add ramping stages, thresholds (http_req_duration p(95)<500, error rate<1%) and check() assertions.

items.prompt:
Review this k6 config and name the exact defect:
export const options = { vus: 500, duration: '10m' };
items.reference:
LABEL: load-test spec defect — fixed 500 VUs dumped in instantly (no ramp/stages) looks like an attack and produces synthetic failures; with no thresholds a saturated p95 still 'passes'.
FIX: stages ramp-up/steady/ramp-down plus thresholds on p95 duration and error rate.
LABEL: no defect — this is a well-formed load test: ramping stages, p95 and error-rate thresholds, and a status check. It can fail, which is the point.

items.prompt: What three things must a load test contain so that it can actually fail and its results are meaningful?
items.reference: LABEL: load-test spec requirements — (1) thresholds tied to the SLO (e.g., p95 http_req_duration < 500ms, error rate < 1%) so the run can fail; (2) checks/assertions on status and body; (3) ramping stages (ramp-up → steady → ramp-down) instead of instant VU counts.

LABEL: unbounded growth (memory leak) — the module-level list grows one entry per request and is never evicted: RSS climbs monotonically until OOM kill.
FIX: deque(maxlen=N), TTL/LRU cache, or persist to a real store.

items.prompt:
Is this handler sound with respect to memory? Name the relevant property:
from collections import deque
history = deque(maxlen=10000)
@app.post('/event')
def event():
    history.append(request.json)
    return 'ok'
items.reference: LABEL: no defect — the buffer is bounded (deque maxlen): memory per process stays constant regardless of traffic, so there is no leak.

LABEL: unbounded cache (memory leak) — the global dict has no TTL and no max size: every new key stays forever, so long-lived processes grow until OOM.
FIX: TTL/LRU cache (maxsize + expiration) or a shared cache (redis).

items.prompt: In production, pod memory climbs during load and never drops after traffic stops. What is the signature and the first code patterns to look for?
items.reference:
LABEL: memory leak signature — RSS growing monotonically with request count and never returning after load stops means unbounded retention, not cache churn.
FIX: hunt module-level lists/dicts appended per request, caches without TTL/max-size, and listeners/connections registered per request and never removed.

LABEL: n+1 queries — the page fires one customer query per order (101 queries): p95 and DB load blow up exactly under traffic.
FIX: single JOIN or one batched IN query (joinedload/select_related) for all referenced ids.

items.prompt:
Is this data access sound? Name the relevant property:
rows = db.execute(
  'SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id')
items.reference: LABEL: no defect — one JOIN returns everything in a single query: query count is constant regardless of page size (no n+1).

items.prompt:
Review this ORM usage and name the exact performance defect:
{% for o in invoice.orders.all %} {{ o.customer.name }} {% endfor %}
items.reference:
LABEL: n+1 queries (lazy loading in template loop) — each iteration triggers a fresh query for customer: a 200-row invoice runs 200+ queries.
FIX: select_related/prefetch (eager load) customers before rendering.

items.prompt: A list endpoint got 20× slower after adding a 'customer_name' column. What is the likely cause and how do you confirm it?
items.reference:
LABEL: n+1 queries — the list endpoint resolves the new customer_name per row, so query count scales with page size.
FIX to confirm: measure by logging/counting queries for one request (query-count middleware) — if count ≈ rows, batch with a JOIN (n+1 confirmed).

LABEL: serial external calls in the request path — one outbound call per user amplifies latency linearly (50 users × 300ms = 15s) and pins workers.
FIX: move the fan-out to a background queue/job with timeouts and retries.
LABEL: no defect — delivery moved off the request path into a background job: the request returns immediately and third-party slowness cannot pin workers.

LABEL: serial external calls (uncached third-party fetch in the request path) — every lookup pays the provider's latency and rate limits; their slowdown becomes your outage.
FIX: short-TTL cache, client timeout, batch where possible, and degrade to last-known price.

items.prompt: p95 jumped from 80ms to 2s but CPU is flat and DB looks idle. What do you suspect and how do you confirm?
items.reference:
LABEL: external dependency latency — with local CPU and DB idle, the time went to an external/third-party call (or DNS) inside the request path.
FIX to confirm: trace one request (span timings), then add a timeout + circuit breaker and cache the call.

LABEL: unbounded result set — the endpoint serializes the whole table per request: memory and response size grow with the table until latency collapses.
FIX: LIMIT/OFFSET or cursor pagination with a bounded page size.
LABEL: no defect — cursor pagination with a hard page cap keeps per-request memory and latency constant regardless of table size.

items.prompt:
Review this search endpoint and name the exact performance defect:
hits = es.search(index='logs', body={'query': q, 'size': 10000})
return hits['hits']['hits']
items.reference:
LABEL: unbounded result set — a 10k-hit page serializes megabytes per request; concurrent large pages OOM the service.
FIX: search_after/cursor pagination, small default page, hard maximum.

items.prompt: An endpoint's latency grows week over week with no code change. Data volume grows too. What do you check first?
items.reference:
LABEL: unbounded result set — if rows served per request grow with the table, serialization/query time grows with data volume.
FIX to confirm: log the response size/row count; if it grows, add pagination (LIMIT/cursor) with a bounded page.

LABEL: overload protection missing — no timeout on the upstream call (a slow upstream pins every worker/connection) and no rate limiting at the edge: one burst collapses the service.
FIX: timeout=(3,10), bounded connection pool, rate limit + circuit breaker, fail fast 503 with retry-after.
LABEL: no defect — bounded timeout on the upstream call plus rate limiting and a connection cap: the service fails fast instead of collapsing.

items.prompt: Under bursts the service returns 502s, workers sit at 100%, and the upstream answers in 8-12s at p95. Name the mechanism.
items.reference:
LABEL: overload collapse — the upstream's p95 exceeds what the proxy tolerates: workers block on slow upstream calls until the pool/worker set is exhausted and the proxy returns 502.
FIX: upstream timeout below the SLO, circuit breaker, bounded concurrency, 503 + retry-after under saturation.

items.prompt: Name the protections that keep a service from collapsing under overload, and what it should do when saturated anyway.
items.reference: LABEL: overload protection set — per-call timeouts, rate limiting, circuit breakers, bounded connection pools and queues (backpressure). When saturated anyway: fail fast with 503 + retry-after instead of queueing forever.

items.prompt: How do you find a service's saturation point (maximum sustainable RPS) with a load test?
items.reference:
LABEL: capacity probe — ramp load in steps and watch p95 latency and error rate per step: the saturation point is the last step where p95 stays within the threshold and errors stay flat.
FIX: record max sustainable RPS vs the latency SLO separately — they are different numbers.

items.prompt: Which latency metric should an SLO use and why not the mean?
items.reference:
LABEL: tail latency — SLOs use p95/p99 because the mean hides the slow tail that real users hit; a mean of 100ms can hide 10% of requests at 2s.
FIX: set SLOs on percentiles (p95/p99) and alert on them, not on averages.

items.prompt: A load test 'passed' every run, including during two outages. What is wrong?
items.reference:
LABEL: load-test spec defect — a test without thresholds cannot fail; it reports green regardless of latency or errors.
FIX: add thresholds tied to the SLO (p95 duration, error rate) so the run fails when the service would hurt users.

items.prompt: A load test shows 5ms p95 in staging but production is 300ms. One likely test defect?
items.reference:
LABEL: cache-flat load — if every request repeats the same payload/URL, the test measures cache hits, not the real path.
FIX: parameterize payloads (unique ids per request) and include the production request mix for a representative result.

items.prompt: p95 correlates with concurrency, not with RPS, and DB CPU is low. What do you check?
items.reference:
LABEL: connection pool starvation — if p95 tracks concurrency while DB CPU is low, requests are queueing on a too-small pool, not on the database.
FIX: raise/bound the pool to match concurrency, measure pool wait time separately, and cap concurrent handlers.

items.prompt: p95 degraded 40% right after a deploy. What is your first diagnostic move?
items.reference:
LABEL: post-deploy regression triage — diff the deploy: new queries (n+1), changed cache keys, new synchronous work in the hot path, dependency changes.
FIX: bisect by re-running the same load against the previous build and profile one request on both to localize the added time.
